title: Video Games and Young People
resolution: Resolved: Video games do more good than harm for young people.
summary: Most American teens play video games. Research finds both benefits and risks, and much of it can't show cause and effect. On balance, do games help young people more than they hurt?

background.p: In a fall 2023 Pew Research Center survey, 85 percent of U.S. teens ages 13 to 17 said they play video games, including 97 percent of boys and about three-quarters of girls. Among teens who play, 56 percent said games have helped their problem-solving skills and 47 percent said they have made a friend online through a game. At the same time, 41 percent said gaming has hurt their sleep, 14 percent of all teens said they spend too much time gaming, and 43 percent of players said they have been harassed or bullied while gaming.

In 2020, the American Psychological Association said there is "insufficient scientific evidence" of a causal link between violent video games and violent behavior, while noting a small, reliable link with milder aggression such as yelling and pushing. The World Health Organization lists "gaming disorder" in its disease classification, ICD-11: a pattern of impaired control over gaming that continues despite harm, usually for at least 12 months. WHO says it affects only a small share of people who play.

Other studies point in different directions, and most have limits. A 2022 study of nearly 2,000 children ages 9 and 10, announced by the National Institutes of Health, found that children who played three or more hours a day did better on tests of impulse control and working memory than children who didn't play, but it couldn't show that gaming caused the difference. A 2022 Oxford study using real play data from about 39,000 adult players found little evidence that time spent playing affected well-being; it studied adults, not children.

disputed.q: Do violent video games make young people more aggressive?
positions: Many studies, summarized by the APA, find a small but reliable link between violent games and aggressive behavior such as yelling and pushing.
Other researchers argue that the link is smaller still or disappears when studies control for other factors, and that it doesn't extend to real violence, as the APA also says.
Some researchers and clinicians see problem gaming as a growing concern, which is why WHO added gaming disorder to ICD-11.
Others argue that the label risks treating heavy but healthy play as illness, and WHO itself says the disorder affects only a small share of players.

terms.def: Two things happening together (correlation) doesn't prove one causes the other (causation). Many gaming studies show only correlation.
A condition in WHO's ICD-11 marked by impaired control over gaming, gaming taking priority over other activities, and continuing despite harm.
A purchase in a game that gives a random reward. Some governments and regulators have examined whether loot boxes work like gambling.
Time spent on any screen. Researchers increasingly study what people do on screens, not only how long.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: For most young people, games build skills, friendships and joy, and the harms fall on a small share who can be helped without losing the benefits for everyone else.

args.warrant: Many games require planning, quick decisions, trial and error and memory. Practicing these skills for fun can carry over to schoolwork and life.
args.evidence: The 2022 NIH-announced study finding better impulse control and working memory in children who game; Pew's finding that 56 percent of teen players say games helped their problem solving.
args.response: The negative answers that the NIH study can't show games caused the difference, since children with stronger skills may simply choose to play more.

args.warrant: Playing together, in the same room or online, gives young people shared goals, teamwork and a way to keep in touch. For shy children it can be an easier way to connect.
args.evidence: Pew (2024): 47 percent of teen players have made a friend online through a game, and 47 percent say games have helped their friendships.
args.response: The negative replies that the same survey found 43 percent of players have been harassed or bullied while gaming, so online play brings risks too.

args.warrant: Games have often been blamed for youth violence, but if the evidence doesn't show games cause violence, that worry shouldn't weigh heavily.
args.evidence: The APA's 2020 statement that evidence doesn't support a causal link between violent games and violent behavior; the NIH-announced study finding no link to increased violence.
args.response: The negative answers that the APA also found a small, reliable link with aggressive behavior, which matters even if it isn't violence.

args.claim: Harms come from too much, not from games.
args.warrant: Lost sleep and problem gaming happen mostly when play crowds out other things. Families can set limits, so the problem is balance, not games.
args.evidence: WHO's statement that gaming disorder affects a small share of players; Pew's finding that most teens say they play the right amount.
args.response: The negative replies that games are designed to keep players playing, so limits are harder to keep than this suggests.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: For many young people, games cost sleep, time and money, expose them to harassment, and are built to be hard to put down; the claimed benefits are uncertain.

args.claim: Games cut into sleep and other activities.
args.warrant: Young people need sleep, exercise, reading and time with family. Hours spent gaming come out of these, and many teens say so themselves.
args.evidence: Pew (2024): 41 percent of teen players say gaming has hurt their sleep, rising to about two-thirds of those who say they play too much; pediatric guidance on sleep.
args.response: The affirmative answers that this is an argument for limits, not against games, and many teens report no sleep problem.

args.claim: Many games are designed to keep players hooked.
args.warrant: Rewards, streaks, random prizes and in-game purchases are built to keep people playing and spending. Young people are less able to resist these designs.
args.evidence: WHO's inclusion of gaming disorder in ICD-11; Federal Trade Commission actions over loot boxes and in-game spending marketed to children, such as a 2025 settlement with a game maker.
args.response: The affirmative replies that many games have no such features, and parents and rules can address the ones that do without condemning all games.

args.claim: Online gaming exposes young people to harassment.
args.warrant: Playing with strangers online means insults, threats and unwanted contact from strangers. These harms can follow children well beyond the game.
args.evidence: Pew (2024): 43 percent of teen players have been harassed or bullied while gaming, 12 percent physically threatened, and 80 percent of teens say harassment over games is a problem for people their age.
args.response: The affirmative answers that this is a problem with online chat, not with games, and that privacy settings and playing with friends reduce it.

args.warrant: Studies showing benefits are mostly correlations, often small, and some study adults. A case for "more good than harm" needs stronger evidence than that.
args.evidence: The limits noted in the NIH-announced study (it can't show cause) and the Oxford study (adult players only, seven games, six weeks).
args.response: The affirmative replies that the evidence for harm has the same limits, so the question comes down to what young people themselves report, which is mostly positive.

strawmen.strawman: They think kids should play games all day.
strawmen.why: Supporters usually favor limits; they argue that games played in balance do more good than harm.
strawmen.steelman: Most young people who play gain thinking skills, friendships and enjoyment, fears about violence aren't supported, and the harms come mostly from excess, which families can manage.

strawmen.strawman: They think video games turn kids into violent criminals.
strawmen.why: Most opponents today argue about sleep, time, design that keeps players hooked, harassment and spending, not violence.
strawmen.steelman: Games often cost young people sleep and time, are designed to be hard to stop, and bring harassment and spending risks, while the claimed benefits rest on weak evidence.

weak.arg: Games are fun, so they must be good.
weak.why: Fun is a real benefit, but it doesn't answer the evidence on sleep, harassment and spending.
It's a slogan, not evidence, and it ignores studies that find no harm or even some benefits to thinking skills.
